seo.title: Muslim-Friendly Korea Tour | Pak Lee's Car
seo.description: A day in Seoul planned around prayer times and genuinely halal food, with the Itaewon mosque on the route. ₩300,000 per vehicle, driver included.

hero.h1: Seoul planned around prayer times and real halal food
hero.lede: The hard part of Korea isn't the sightseeing, it's lunch. Plenty of places put a halal sign in the window without a certificate behind it. I know which ones are certified, which are Muslim-owned, and where you can pray without hunting for somewhere quiet.

itinerary.title: Pickup, and we check the times
itinerary.body: Before we set off I look at today's Zuhur and Asr times and build the driving around them, so you're near somewhere suitable rather than stuck in traffic when they come.

itinerary.title: Gyeongbokgung
itinerary.body: The guard changing is at 10:00, and the palace is closed on Tuesdays. It's flat, shaded in parts, and there is a quiet corner near the west side that works if a prayer falls here.

itinerary.title: Itaewon: Seoul Central Mosque and lunch
itinerary.body: The mosque is on the hill above the main road, open to visitors outside prayer times, with a women's section upstairs. The street below it is where the certified halal restaurants are — Turkish, Pakistani, Uzbek and a Korean place doing halal bulgogi.

itinerary.title: Namsan and N Seoul Tower
itinerary.body: Ten minutes from Itaewon. I drive up to the terminus and you take the cable car for the last stretch, so it's a short walk rather than the full climb.

itinerary.title: Myeongdong
itinerary.body: There's a small prayer room near the shopping streets and several halal-certified street stalls, though not every cart is one. I'll point out which is which before you queue.

itinerary.title: Dinner, then your hotel
itinerary.body: Back to Itaewon for a proper sit-down meal, or a certified Korean barbecue in Jongno if you want the grill experience. Then straight to your door.

faqs.q: How do you know a restaurant is really halal?
faqs.a: Korea has a certification scheme, and separately there are Muslim-owned restaurants that everyone in the community knows. I use those two, not the window stickers. Where a place is only 'Muslim-friendly' — no pork, but alcohol served — I'll tell you that plainly and let you decide.

faqs.q: Where can we pray during the day?
faqs.a: Seoul Central Mosque in Itaewon is the main one, and there are small prayer rooms in Myeongdong, at Incheon Airport and in a few department stores. I keep a mat in the car as well.

faqs.q: Can you do this during Ramadan?
faqs.a: Yes, and the day looks different: a later start, sightseeing in the cooler hours, and being at a restaurant before Maghrib rather than after. Tell me you're fasting and I'll plan it that way.
No. I'm a Korean driver who has taken a lot of Indonesian and Malaysian families around, and I've learned where things are by asking my guests and going with them.

faqs.q: Can we go somewhere outside Seoul instead?
faqs.a: Yes. Nami Island and Everland both have halal options nearby and I can plan either the same way. Nami is a longer drive, so the day is priced differently.
No, per vehicle. ₩300,000 covers the van and me for ten hours, whether you are a couple or a family of eight.

reels.body: Short clips from days with families like yours.

cta.body: Tell me your dates and how strict you'd like me to be about the food. I'll plan the day around it.
